notes: High acidity is the hallmark of German wine, from a northern climate and grapes like Riesling that keep acid even when ripe.
Riesling ranges from very crisp and dry through off-dry (feinherb or halbtrocken) to rich, sweet Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese.
In 2025, 53% of German quality and Prädikat wine was dry.
Riesling ages well, gaining smoky, honey and petrol notes.
Dornfelder gives dark, full bodied, fruity and tannic reds.
Baden, Germany's warmest region, makes wines that are usually fuller bodied and higher in alcohol than elsewhere in Germany.
Its Pinot Blanc and Pinot Gris are among the most powerful in Germany.
Franken is known for powerful, dry Silvaner from chalky soils, slightly earthy and rustic.
Its best wines, mostly dry Spätlesen, are full bodied and can mature for six to ten years.
Fränkisch trocken is reserved for Franken wines with no more than 4 grams of fermentable sugar per liter.
Mosel Riesling is often light, low in alcohol, crisp and high in acidity, with flowery as well as fruity aromas.
High acidity and clearly defined flavors mark all Mosel wines, and some sweetness often balances the acid.
Saar and Ruwer wines can be just 6 to 9% alcohol, with intense fruit and high acidity.
The Mosel is also known for Eiswein, joining high acidity to concentrated sweetness.
Nahe wines show wet stone and mineral flavors with citrus and stone fruit.
Pfalz wines are traditionally dry and full bodied.
Riesling here can develop citrus and peach notes, and its Pinot Blanc and Pinot Gris are among Germany's most powerful.
About three quarters of the Rheingau is Riesling, whose long ripening here gives fine acidity and delicate aromas.
Rheinhessen makes mostly white wine from Riesling, Müller-Thurgau and Silvaner.
Silvaner from chalky soils gives powerful dry wines, slightly earthy and rustic.
